strengths: The core idea of replacing discrete-token communication between stacked/multiple LLM modules with continuous dense-vector passing is conceptually clean, well motivated by the redundancy of embedding/de-embedding, and is presented with a clear formalism (Section 3) including a straightforward end-to-end differentiability argument (Proposition 1).

The parameter-efficient customization experiments (Section 5.2.2, Table 4) provide a genuinely more controlled comparison: with a fixed backbone (GPT2-M) and comparable added-parameter budgets, LMNet variants are competitive with or exceed standard PEFT baselines (Adapters, Prefix-tuning, LoRA), and can be composed with LoRA/Prefix for further gains, illustrating real versatility of the framework.

The complexity analysis (Section 4.3) and discussion of topology/vertex-sharing options are reasonably thorough for a conceptual contribution, and the paper is transparent that it presents 'the basic idea and primary practice' rather than a fully polished system.

The attention-weight visualizations and attempts at interpretability (Section 5.1.2, Appendix A), while inconclusive, represent an honest effort to probe what the learned edges are doing rather than only reporting benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: The headline claim that LMNet-1B matches similarly-sized LLMs at '<0.1% training cost' is misleading: the vertex module is a fully pre-trained Qwen2.5-0.5B model that already consumed 18T tokens of training; the 0.01T-token edge training is layered on top of this already-expensive asset, so the fair comparison is not '0.1% of from-scratch training cost' but rather 'additional continued training of an existing model,' which is a much weaker and less novel claim than advertised in the abstract and conclusion.

No ablation isolates the actual source of improvement: it is not shown whether simply continuing to pre-train/fine-tune the single Qwen2.5-0.5B vertex model on the same 0.01T-token data mixture (without the LMNet graph structure/edges) would achieve similar gains. Without this baseline, the paper cannot support its central claim that dense vector communication between multiple LLM copies—rather than additional training compute/data on the base model—drives the reported improvements.

Inference-time computational cost is never analyzed. LMNet-1B invokes the 0.5B vertex transformer repeatedly across a 5-layer, width-4 topology; even with weight sharing and layer-wise parallelism, this likely incurs substantially higher FLOPs/latency per generated token than the single dense baselines in Table 1, yet the comparison table only reports parameter count and training tokens, omitting the inference overhead that is critical for a fair 'efficiency' claim.

The interpretability analysis in Section 5.1.2 is largely inconclusive (de-embedding intermediate vectors 'failed' to produce meaningful text; the topology visualizations show no discernible pattern), which weakens confidence that the system is doing something qualitatively different from a deep, weight-tied network with extra trainable adapters.

Section 4.4 and parts of the conclusion make speculative, unsupported claims about emergent reasoning and collective intelligence ('it can be expected that LMNet ... fosters emergent behaviors ... that transcend the capabilities of its individual components') without any evidence in the experiments to substantiate such claims.

Mixed results on GSM8K (Table 3), where LMNet underperforms simple prompting for stronger backbones, and inconsistent gains across benchmarks/backbones somewhat undercut the versatility narrative, though the paper does discuss this openly.

Reproducibility is limited: hyperparameters (learning rates, optimizer, exact training schedule split between edge-only and joint optimization phases, exact data subset sizes/mixture ratios) are not fully specified, and code is only promised for future release rather than provided with the submission.

The novelty of the technical realization is somewhat incremental: connecting weight-shared transformer blocks via lightweight trainable attention adapters and jointly fine-tuning is conceptually similar to existing depth-extension/model-stacking and adapter-based techniques; the 'dense vector communication between LLMs' framing, while evocative, is not clearly differentiated from simply inserting additional transformer/adapter layers between repeated copies of a pretrained model.
Minor presentation issues include repeated/duplicated sentences (e.g., in Section 5.2.1 the same sentence about model strength appears twice) and occasional grammatical errors that reduce polish.

strengths: The core idea of exploring differentiable, dense-vector communication between LLM modules (bypassing embedding/de-embedding) is conceptually interesting and distinct from the dominant natural-language multi-agent paradigm.

The paper provides a clear formalization (Proposition 1, complexity analysis) of end-to-end differentiability and parameter/time complexity under weight sharing, which is a reasonable theoretical contribution.

Section 5.2.2 (E2E dataset, GPT2-M) is a relatively well-controlled experiment: parameter budgets for LMNet variants are roughly matched against a standard suite of PEFT baselines (Adapter, Prefix, LoRA), and LMNet shows competitive or better results, and shows the framework composes with existing PEFT methods (LoRA, Prefix).
The paper is reasonably transparent about limited compute budget and explicitly frames LMNet-1B as a proof-of-concept rather than a ready-to-use model.
weaknesses: The headline claim ('comparable performance with <0.1% training cost') is misleading: LMNet-1B's vertex weights are initialized from a Qwen2.5-0.5B model already pretrained on 18T tokens, so the 0.01T-token 'training cost' ignores the enormous prior investment already baked into the reused backbone. Comparing this to models trained entirely from scratch is an apples-to-oranges comparison that substantially overstates the claimed efficiency gain.

In the main scaling experiment (5.1.1), all vertices share a single pretrained model (Qwen2.5-0.5B); there is no experiment with genuinely different LLMs as different vertices. This undercuts the central 'communication between LLMs' / collective-intelligence narrative, since the system is effectively one model duplicated with extra trainable inter-layer transforms rather than multiple distinct agents collaborating.

No baselines isolate what specifically drives the reported gains (e.g., simple continued pretraining/fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-0.5B on the same extra tokens, or naive layer-stacking/depth-expansion of the same backbone with the same added parameter budget and token budget). Without such ablations, it is impossible to attribute improvement to the proposed 'dense communication' mechanism rather than simply added parameters and continued training.

The interpretability/mechanistic analysis in 5.1.2 is largely a negative result presented optimistically: de-embedding intermediate dense vectors produces non-English, uninterpretable outputs, and the only positive evidence offered (attention-weight differences across 4 edges in Figure 3, and qualitatively similar projection-matrix visualizations in Appendix A) is weak and does not substantiate claims of meaningful 'machine-native' communication or emergent reasoning protocols.

Mixed and sometimes negative results are downplayed: on GSM8K (Table 3), LMNet underperforms simple prompting for two of four backbones (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B), and the explanation offered is post-hoc and speculative rather than empirically verified.

Reproducibility is limited: no code, configs, or detailed hyperparameters accompany the submission (code 'will be released'), training/eval details (exact schedules, data mixture proportions, seeds) are sparse, and all reported numbers appear to be single-run point estimates with no variance/error bars.

Presentation issues suggest insufficient proofreading (e.g., duplicated sentences in Section 5.2.1 explaining GSM8K results), and some claims (e.g., 'exploration of capabilities beyond human heuristics', 'machine-native communication') are asserted rhetorically without concrete supporting evidence.

The broader significance claim—that this offers 'a new perspective on scaling for general intelligence'—is not adequately supported at the scale tested (sub-2B parameter models, small topologies of 3-5 layers, narrow benchmark set); the extrapolation to large-scale collective intelligence remains speculative.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually interesting and clearly articulated idea: replacing discrete-token communication between LLM modules with direct dense-vector communication, avoiding embedding/de-embedding round-trips and yielding a fully differentiable, MLP-like multi-model architecture (LMNet).

The theoretical formulation is clean: stripping embedding/de-embedding layers, defining vertex/edge composition, and proving end-to-end differentiability (Proposition 1) is presented with sufficient rigor and clarity for reproducibility of the architecture.

The customization experiments on the E2E dataset (Table 4) provide a genuinely controlled, apples-to-apples comparison against well-established PEFT baselines (LoRA, Adapter, Prefix-tuning) at matched parameter budgets, and show LMNet variants performing competitively or better, while also being composable with LoRA/Prefix — this is the most convincing evidence in the paper.

The paper explores multiple application scenarios (scaling from pretrained components, low-resource domain adaptation on MMLU/GSM8K, and PEFT-style customization), showing some versatility of the proposed mechanism.
Reasonably honest acknowledgment of limited compute budget and explicit discussion of future directions (larger vertex diversity, alternative topologies, RL integration).
weaknesses: The headline claim that LMNet-1B matches or beats similarly-sized LLMs with '<0.1% training cost' (Table 1, Section 5.1) is misleading: the vertex module is Qwen2.5-0.5B, already pretrained on 18T tokens, so the '0.01T token' figure ignores the enormous pretraining investment already embedded in the shared vertex weights. The comparison is not a fair test of the dense-communication paradigm's efficiency versus training a model from scratch, and the framing overstates the contribution.

The core motivating claim — that dense-vector communication is more efficient/effective than natural-language communication between LLMs — is never directly tested. There is no controlled ablation comparing LMNet-style dense communication against an equivalent system where the same vertices communicate via discrete tokens/natural language under matched compute and parameter budgets, leaving the central hypothesis of the paper empirically unverified.

No ablation isolates whether gains in Table 1 stem from the proposed communication mechanism versus simply having more effective parameters/depth from replicating a pretrained model and further training it (e.g., missing baselines: continued pretraining of Qwen2.5-0.5B alone on the same 0.01T tokens, naive depth-stacking/duplication of the same model and fine-tuning, or simple ensembling of multiple copies).

Potential data leakage/contamination concern: the LMNet pretraining set explicitly includes MMLU auxiliary_training, MATH training split, and GSM8K training split, and the model is then evaluated on MMLU, MATH, and GSM8K test/eval sets in the same table where it is compared against baseline LLMs that were not tuned on these exact benchmark training distributions — this asymmetry could substantially inflate LMNet's relative benchmark scores independent of any architectural benefit.

Mixed and partially unfavorable results undercut the generality of the approach: on GSM8K (Table 3), LMNet underperforms simple prompting for stronger backbones (Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B), and the paper's own diagnostic analysis (Section 5.1.2) failed to produce interpretable evidence of a meaningful learned communication protocol (de-embedding attempts failed entirely, and the sole positive finding — that different edges show different attention patterns — is a fairly trivial observation).

Single training run per setting with no repeated seeds, variance estimates, or statistical significance analysis, which is concerning given the small-scale, limited-budget experiments (≤60 GPU-days) that underlie the strongest claims in the paper.

Presentation issues remain: duplicated/garbled sentences in Section 5.2.1, and awkward phrasing in Section 2 ('Given training data from the specific domain to for data-driven customization... [54] that.'), suggesting insufficient proofreading of a paper making strong claims.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to cited prior work on continuous-space reasoning (COCONUT) and differentiable multi-agent communication (Sukhbaatar et al.), with the main new element being the MLP-like layered topology and reuse of pretrained LLMs as shared nodes; this architectural contribution alone, absent the rigorous efficiency comparison, is a relatively modest advance.

strengths: Novel and clear conceptual framing ("language model networks") that unifies test-time scaling, multi-agent systems, and latent reasoning under a common topology/communication/optimization lens, offering a useful vocabulary for the community.

The core technical idea—stripping intermediate embedding/de-embedding layers and inserting trainable seq2seq edge modules to enable dense, differentiable inter-model communication in an MLP-like fully-connected topology—is a reasonable and non-trivial extension of prior latent-reasoning work (COCONUT, CODI) to richer, non-chain topologies.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span multiple benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, BBH, ARC-C, TruthfulQA, GSM8K, MATH, GPQA, HumanEval, MBPP, E2E) and multiple backbones (GPT2, Llama3.2, Qwen2.5 at various sizes), with comparisons to SFT, prompting/ICL/CoT, PEFT methods (LoRA, Prefix, Adapters), TTS baselines (Self-Consistency, Self-Refine), and latent-reasoning baselines (COCONUT, CODI).
Practical engineering contribution of vertex parameter sharing to control parameter/latency growth, with an explicit complexity analysis.

Attempt at interpretability/analysis of learned communication (macro-level parameter statistics across edges, micro-level case study of de-embedded intermediate representations), which is a good-faith effort to open the black box.

Honest and fairly detailed limitations section acknowledging complexity, black-box-API incompatibility, reduced interpretability, and the gap between the current end-to-end autoregressive implementation and the motivating vision of sentence-level dense messaging.
weaknesses: Key scaling claim is not well supported by the paper's own data: Table 7 shows LMNet-1B actually underperforms the similarly-sized Qwen2.5-1.5B on most benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, ARC-C, GSM8K, GPQA, MMLU-stem, HumanEval, MBPP), yet the text claims "comparable or even better performance," which overstates the result.

The main capability-improvement comparison (Table 1) is confounded: LMNet combines both additional trained parameters (~0.6B edge modules trained on task-relevant data) and 14x more forward computation, but is compared against untrained TTS baselines (Self-Consistency/Self-Refine) applied to the same frozen 0.5B model at matched sample budget; this does not isolate whether gains stem from the proposed dense-communication mechanism versus simply added trainable capacity and compute.

The SFT baseline in Table 1 shows a performance *decrease* (-5.7%) from the pre-trained model, which is unusual and suggests the SFT baseline may be poorly tuned, undermining confidence in the comparison used to argue that gains come from communication rather than training data.

No variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing is reported anywhere, despite training being described as noisy/limited-budget (100 GPU-days, <0.02T tokens); single-run numbers are used to support strong claims (e.g., +30.5% relative improvement).

The interpretability analysis in Appendix B is a single anecdotal case study (one GSM8K example) plus unlabeled parameter-matrix visualizations without quantitative metrics, which is insufficient to substantiate claims about "nontrivial communication behaviors" or that the fully-connected topology is meaningfully exploited rather than acting as redundant computation.

Reproducibility is limited: the code repository link is left blank/placeholder, training/data mixture details for the main capability experiment are only partially specified, and compute constraints mean only very small-scale networks (few layers/vertices) are validated, leaving open whether findings scale to more realistic settings.

The ablation on depth/width (Table 6) shows no significant or consistent pattern, which somewhat undercuts the motivation for the specific MLP-inspired fully-connected topology chosen as the default architecture.

The framing of the contribution as a new general paradigm is broad, but the concrete realization (end-to-end autoregressive training over a fixed fully-connected graph) is acknowledged by the authors themselves (Section 6.3, Limitations) to not match the motivating picture of learned sentence-level agent communication, making the central narrative and the implemented method somewhat misaligned.

strengths: The paper offers an appealing unifying conceptual framing ('language model networks') that connects test-time scaling, multi-agent systems, and latent reasoning as instances of a common topology/communication/optimization design space.

The core technical idea—stripping embedding/de-embedding layers so intermediate LLM nodes exchange dense hidden states instead of discrete tokens, enabling end-to-end gradient flow—is a reasonable and moderately novel extension beyond single-chain latent reasoning methods (COCONUT, CODI) toward richer, learnable topologies.
The parameter-sharing and lightweight edge-module design is a sensible engineering choice that keeps additional parameter/compute overhead small relative to the number of 'virtual' nodes.

Fairly broad experimental coverage: general-capability improvement, low-resource task adaptation (MMLU/GSM8K/E2E), comparisons against PEFT methods, latent-reasoning baselines, and test-time-scaling baselines, plus ablations on vertex size and depth/width.

The limitations section is candid, e.g. explicitly acknowledging (Sec 6.3) that the current end-to-end autoregressive implementation does not realize the motivating 'sentence-level machine communication' picture and that gains may stem from extra test-time computation rather than the advertised mechanism.
weaknesses: Central causal claim is undermined by the authors' own admission (Sec 6.3, Appendix B.2): intermediate dense messages mostly fail to decode into anything meaningful, and the authors state the performance gain 'should be attributed to more test-time computation' rather than to learned dense communication protocols, which contradicts the paper's main motivating narrative and headline contributions.

The flagship 'general capability' experiment (Table 1, Sec 4.1) is not an iso-compute/iso-training comparison: LMNet is trained end-to-end with additional parameters and public data, while the Self-Consistency/Self-Refine baselines simply run the untrained backbone more times at test time. This confounds the effect of 'learned dense communication' with the effect of additional trainable parameters and additional training data, so the claimed +30.5% vs +0.5%/+3.4% advantage does not isolate the mechanism the paper argues for.

The SFT baseline in Table 1 (-5.7% relative to the untrained backbone) is suspicious and only loosely justified as due to 'very moderate training configurations' and data already seen in pretraining; without hyperparameter/training details this looks like a weak baseline that inflates LMNet's apparent advantage.

All experiments are at very small scale (≤7B vertex models, <0.02T additional tokens, <100 GPU-days), and the comparison with fully pretrained LLMs of similar size (Appendix A) pits a minimally-trained LMNet against models trained on 15-18T tokens; while the authors caveat this, it still leaves open whether the core mechanism has any benefit at realistic scale or under a fair training-compute budget.

The topology ablation (Table 6) explicitly reports 'no significant difference or patterns' across depths/widths on E2E, undercutting the paper's central architectural claim that the layer-wise fully-connected topology (analogous to MLP universal approximation) is important; no similarly controlled topology ablation is provided for the flagship general-capability experiment.

The qualitative/interpretability analysis in Appendix B is thin: a single case study and coarse statistical observations about parameter matrices ('edges are different from random init, no clear pattern') that provide little rigorous evidence about what is actually being learned or why it helps.

Results are inconsistent across settings: in the low-data GSM8K regime (Table 9, Appendix C) LMNet underperforms simple prompting for two of four backbones, and the paper only 'fixes' this by adding substantial extra training data (93.7k examples) in the main text while relegating the failure case to the appendix, which reads as selective reporting.

Key reproducibility details (learning rates, batch sizes, optimizer settings, exact training schedules, data splits/sizes per experiment) are largely missing from both the main text and appendices, and the code link is a placeholder, making it hard to verify or reproduce the reported numbers.

The paper repeatedly hedges that it 'aims to provide a method rather than the trained LMNet ready-to-use,' which is used to excuse several inconclusive or unfavorable comparisons rather than being resolved with additional rigorous experiments.

strengths: The paper offers a clean and useful conceptual unification, framing test-time scaling, multi-agent systems, latent reasoning, and workflow optimization as instances of a common 'language model network' paradigm, differentiated by topology, communication medium, and optimization strategy.

The core technical idea, stripping intermediate embedding/de-embedding layers so stripped-transformer vertices exchange dense vectors through trainable seq2seq edge modules, is a reasonably clean way to make inter-model communication end-to-end differentiable, and the parameter-sharing analysis (Section 3.3) gives a sensible account of how complexity can be controlled.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad: general-capability improvement across many benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, BBH, ARC-C, TruthfulQA, GSM8K, MATH, GPQA, HumanEval, MBPP), limited-supervision adaptation on MMLU/GSM8K/E2E, comparisons against PEFT methods, latent-reasoning baselines (COCONUT, CODI), and TTS baselines (Self-Refine, Self-Consistency), plus ablations over vertex model size and network depth/width.

The paper includes an honest and fairly deep self-critical discussion (Sections 6.3 and 7), explicitly noting that the current end-to-end autoregressive training does not realize the envisioned sentence-level dense message-passing, and that de-embedded intermediate vectors are not human-interpretable — a limitation many papers would obscure.
The macro/micro-level analysis of the trained network's communication behavior (Appendix B) is a nice addition that goes beyond aggregate metrics to inspect what the learned edges are actually doing.
weaknesses: The central 'multi-model collective intelligence' framing is arguably overclaimed relative to what is implemented: because vertex parameters are shared across all nodes, the system reduces largely to inserting additional trainable interleaved transformer-like blocks (the edge modules) between repeated forward passes of a single shared backbone, more akin to architecturally deepening/widening a single model than to genuine communication between distinct 'language model' agents. This conflates 'added trainable depth/parameters trained end-to-end' with the paper's 'network of reusable LM nodes' narrative.

Baseline fairness is questionable: the SFT baseline actually degrades performance relative to the untouched pretrained model (-5.7%) in the main capability experiment, which is unusual for public-data fine-tuning and suggests the baseline may not have been well-tuned (learning rate, schedule, regularization), inflating LMNet's relative improvement.

Reproducibility is weak: the code link in Section 4 is blank/broken ('Code is provided at .'), and many training details (learning rates, optimizer, number of steps, exact data mixtures/sizes used from each corpus) are not fully specified, especially for the large capability-improvement experiment.

All experiments use small models (0.5B–7B parameters) and modest compute budgets (e.g., <100 GPU-days, <0.02T tokens for the main capability claim); no results demonstrate the approach at scales more representative of modern LLM deployments, and no error bars or multiple seeds are reported to assess variance of the reported gains.

The comparison to monolithic pretrained LLMs in Table 7 (e.g., vs. Llama3.2-1B/3B trained on 15T tokens from scratch) is somewhat apples-to-oranges since the LMNet vertex already benefits from Qwen2.5-0.5B's full 18T-token pretraining plus additional fine-tuning; the 'less than 0.2% of pretraining cost' framing risks overstating efficiency by ignoring the amortized cost of the base model's original pretraining.

Appendix C reveals that on the original, unaugmented GSM8K training set, LMNet actually underperforms simple Prompting for two of four backbone LLMs (Table 9), and only shows a clear advantage after adding 93.7k extra math training examples; this weakens the 'supervision-efficient adaptation' claim and suggests the benefits are sensitive to data scale in ways not fully explored.

The claimed advantage over TTS methods (Self-Consistency/Self-Refine) at matched inference-time budget does not account for the substantial additional training cost LMNet requires (full end-to-end gradient optimization) versus the training-free nature of the TTS baselines, making the comparison asymmetric in an unacknowledged way.

Only a single topology (layer-wise fully-connected, MLP-like) is empirically evaluated despite the paper's broader claims about a general 'language model networks' paradigm encompassing diverse topologies; alternative topologies are discussed only conceptually in Section 6.2, without experiments.
